rules.statement: Add a new section to a composable discovery or capabilities document by registering a new provider (e.g. an `ICommandHandler` the mediator fans out to), never by editing the endpoint or the document's resource type.
rules.why: The document is composed from registered parts so that sibling packages can extend it without anyone modifying the endpoint.
rules.check: Look for diffs that add capability data by changing the endpoint handler or adding properties to the extension-data resource type when they should add a registered provider.

rules.statement: Don't keep per-type lists of key types, algorithms, key sizes or curves duplicated across generators, validators, converters or clients; derive them from the registered key-type descriptors and algorithm catalog.
rules.why: Each copy can drift from the others. With registered descriptors, a new key type shows up everywhere without any other edit.
rules.check: Look for hard-coded switch statements, arrays or enums listing secret types, algorithms or curves outside the registered descriptors, including in client or console code that should read the capabilities document.

rules.statement: Don't serve a document that describes a deployment's key management services, algorithms or secret types to anonymous callers; require an authenticated caller unless a client must read it before it can get a token (as with OpenID discovery).
rules.why: An anonymous survey of the deployment's key services and algorithms is reconnaissance, and no anonymous consumer needs the document.
rules.check: Look for capability or configuration-describing endpoints that allow anonymous access or skip the authenticated-caller check.

rules.statement: When a management route needs an authenticated caller but no valid access token is present, return the shared authentication-required `401` problem document that every other route uses, not a custom response.
rules.why: Every management route gives the same `401` problem document when the caller has no valid token, so clients can handle it the same way everywhere.
rules.check: Look for handlers that build their own 401 response or problem details instead of calling the shared authentication-required problem factory.

rules.statement: A route that requires authentication but performs no authority check declares `401` and not `403` in its OpenAPI problem declarations, and the route-declaration test lists it among the authenticated-caller routes.
rules.why: A route with no authority check cannot answer `403`, so declaring it would be false, and the host walk test keeps the declaration accurate.
rules.check: Compare the route's declared problem status codes with its handler: a `403` declared without any authority or role check is a violation, as is a new authenticated route missing from the route-declaration test.
